title: Ayyub's du'a
hookLine: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful (21:83)

cards: Hospital waiting rooms have their own language. Some people go silent. Some rage.
Some bargain: if you fix this, I'll do anything. Ayyub, Job, was struck by illness, and commentators say he lost his wealth and his family too.
Stories people tell describe years of it, in vivid detail; the Qur'an gives no number and no gore. What it does give is the prayer he finally prays. A single verse, and it doesn't ask for anything.

teach.b: Surah al-Anbiya, verse eighty-three, in Pickthall's translation: Ayyub cries to his Lord, "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy."
In Arabic: anni massaniya d-durr, wa anta arhamu r-rahimin. Two statements, side by side. Harm has touched me.
And You are the most merciful of the merciful. That's all. He doesn't say heal me, or why me.
He doesn't list what he's lost. He tells the truth about his pain and the truth about Allah, and leaves the two next to each other.

teach.h: ADAB: SAY THE NEED, NAME THE MERCY.
teach.b: Scholars have long pointed to this as a model of courtesy in asking, adab: the need laid out, the mercy named, and the One who's merciful trusted to connect them.
The verb is massa, to touch: harm has touched me, the Qur'an's ordinary word for affliction reaching someone, used without drama.

The next verse gives the answer: We heard him, removed the harm, and restored his family to him, and the like of them with them, a mercy from Us and a reminder for those who worship. Surah Sad adds the scene.
He's told: strike the ground with your foot; here is cool water to wash in and to drink. And Allah describes him: We found him patient; how excellent a servant; he was always turning back.
Patience, in Ayyub, isn't silence. It's saying the hard thing and the true thing in one breath, and not letting go of either.

how: Muslims who are ill, or praying for someone who is, often recite Ayyub's du'a (21:83); visiting the sick is a strongly encouraged practice in Islam.

o: heal me now, and give back what I lost
harm has touched me; You are most merciful
why me, after all my years of worship

p: We heard him and removed the harm

s: Ayyub's du'a asks Allah directly to heal him
he names the harm and names Allah's mercy, and asks nothing more.
the Qur'an says how many years Ayyub suffered
it gives no number; the long accounts come from stories people tell.
Allah calls Ayyub patient and an excellent servant
surah Sad: We found him patient; how excellent a servant.

games.q: you're Ayyub. health, wealth and family are gone. you finally pray. what do you say?
o: heal me now, and I'll do anything.
harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful.
games.why: he names the harm and names the mercy, and Allah hears him and removes the harm (21:83–84).

practice: Let someone who is ill come to mind, in body, in mind, or in grief, and picture them where they are right now, a bed, a waiting room, a kitchen, without rushing to fix it.
If you pray, recite Ayyub's own words from 21:83 while you hold them in mind; if you don't, hold both truths: they're hurting, and they're not alone.

wordCard.voice: Ayyub's du'a. Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful: a prayer that names the pain and the mercy, and asks nothing more. Today's word.
